# Fertilizer Field Trial — OLS Regression Analysis

## Overview

We analysed a field trial of 40 wheat plots spanning nitrogen fertilizer doses of
0–200 kg ha⁻¹ (yield measured in t ha⁻¹). An ordinary least-squares (OLS) simple
linear regression of yield on fertilizer dose was fitted using Python (scipy.stats.linregress).

## Regression Results

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| slope = 0.0151 t ha⁻¹ per kg ha⁻¹ | |
| intercept = 1.753 t ha⁻¹ | |
| R^2 = 0.921 | |
| p-value | < 0.001 |
| Std. error of slope | 0.00272 |
| n | 40 |

**Fitted model:**

> yield = 0.0151 × fertilizer_dose + 1.753

## Interpretation

**Slope (slope = 0.0151):** For each additional kilogram of nitrogen fertilizer
applied per hectare, wheat yield increases by approximately 0.015 t ha⁻¹. Over the
full observed dose range (0–200 kg ha⁻¹) this translates to a predicted yield gain
of roughly 3.0 t ha⁻¹.

**Intercept (1.753 t ha⁻¹):** The model predicts a baseline yield of ≈ 1.75 t ha⁻¹
for unfertilized plots, consistent with the observed zero-dose yields (1.14–2.73 t ha⁻¹).

**Goodness of fit (R^2 = 0.921):** Fertilizer dose explains approximately **92 %**
of the variance in wheat yield across the 40 plots. This is a strong dose–response
relationship; the linear model captures the overwhelming majority of yield variability,
indicating that nitrogen application rate is the dominant driver of yield in this
trial. The highly significant p-value (< 0.001) confirms that the association is
extremely unlikely to arise by chance.

## Conclusion

The OLS regression provides strong evidence that nitrogen fertilizer dose is an
excellent linear predictor of wheat yield in this dataset (R^2 = 0.921, slope = 0.0151,
p < 0.001). Growers can expect roughly 15 kg of additional grain per additional
kilogram of nitrogen applied per hectare under conditions similar to this trial.
